A lesson on the Incense Routes

Getting frankincense and myrrh from Arabia to Europe

Yemen and Oman are the only places nearby where frankincense and myrrh trees grow. This map shows two ways to carry the goods north toward the Mediterranean: Alia's journey, and the Frankincense Road. Compare the terrain each one crosses.

1. Two routes, two kinds of terrain

Toggle each route below to highlight it on the map, and read what the ground underfoot is actually like along the way.

2. Towns along the Frankincense Road — the desert's ports

A caravan couldn't just cross the desert in one push. It needed the same things a ship needs from a port: water, shelter, supplies, and somewhere to pay its dues before moving on. Click each town to see what it offered.

💧 Water ⛰ Shelter / lodging 🌾 Fodder for camels 💰 Tolls & taxes 🛡 Guides & guards 🛒 Market / trade goods
Click a town on the map to see what it offered a passing caravan.

3. Why go overland at all?

Ships were faster in theory. So why did merchants stick to camel caravans for most of the incense trade's history, only shifting to the Red Sea in the 1st century CE?

The case for the caravan

  • Camels were domesticated for desert transport by roughly 2000 BCE — long before anyone understood the monsoon wind patterns needed to sail the Red Sea safely.
  • The Frankincense Road had centuries of built infrastructure: wells, fodder stations, guides, and armed guards who knew every oasis and taxation point along the named towns on the map.
  • Kingdoms along the route (Saba, Qataban, the Nabataeans) had a direct financial stake in keeping caravans moving — and taxed, but protected, them.
  • A camel could carry roughly 500 lb and survive nearly a week without water — built for exactly this terrain.

The case against the sea

  • The Red Sea was called a navigational nightmare: fierce storms, chains of reefs, and submerged islands, with no maps.
  • Early Egyptian expeditions to Punt had to build ships on the Nile, take them apart, drag the pieces across 100 miles of desert, then reassemble them at the coast.
  • Losing a shipment to a reef meant losing the entire cargo at once — a caravan spread risk across many camels and drivers instead.
  • A land route could be taxed, guarded, and rerouted around trouble; a ship in open water couldn't call for help.

4. The maritime route — and its hazards

Once merchants did commit to the sea, the Red Sea leg from southern Arabia up to Egyptian ports was the most dangerous stretch of the whole journey. Click each marker on the map to see why.
